problems.question: Jamie counted the number of edges of a cube, Jimmy counted the number of corners, and Judy counted the number of faces. They then added the three numbers. What was the resulting sum?
hints: A cube has a fixed number of edges, corners, and faces.
Add the counts for edges, corners, and faces.
problems.solution: A cube has \(12\) edges, \(8\) corners, and \(6\) faces. Adding these together yields \[ 12 + 8 + 6 = 26. \] Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Which of the following numbers has the smallest prime factor?
hints: Look for a number with prime factor \(2.\)
Among the choices, only one is even.
problems.solution: Note that the smallest prime number is \(2.\) This means that any even number would be our answer. Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: A burger at Ricky C’s weighs \(120\) grams, of which \(30\) grams are filler. What percent of the burger is not filler?
hints: First find how many grams are not filler.
Compare the non-filler grams to \(120.\)
problems.solution: We get that \(120 - 30 = 90\) grams are not filler. The percentage is therefore \[ 100 \cdot \dfrac{90}{120} = 100 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} = 75 \%. \] Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: A group of children riding on bicycles and tricycles rode past Billy Bob’s house. Billy Bob counted \(7\) children and \(19\) wheels. How many tricycles were there?
hints: If all \(7\) children had bicycles, count the wheels.
Each tricycle adds one wheel compared with a bicycle.
problems.solution: Let \(b\) be the number of bicycles and \(t\) be the number of tricycles. Then we can set up the following system of equations: \[ \begin{gather*} b + t = 7, \\ 2b + 3t = 19. \end{gather*} \] Multiplying the first equation by \(2\) and subtracting from the second equation, we get \(t = 5.\) Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: If \(20 \%\) of a number is \(12,\) what is \(30\%\) of the same number?
hints: \(20\%\) is one fifth.
Use \(10\%\) as a stepping stone from \(20\%\) to \(30\%.\)
problems.solution: Since \(20\%\) of the number is \(12,\) \(10\%\) of the number is \(6.\) Therefore \(30\%\) of the same number is \(3\cdot6=18.\) Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Given the areas of the three squares in the figure, what is the area of the interior triangle?
hints: The square areas give the side lengths of the three squares.
The side lengths form a \(5-12-13\) right triangle.
problems.solution: The side lengths of the squares are \[ \sqrt{169} = 13,\]\[ \sqrt{144} = 12, \] and \[ \sqrt{25} = 5. \] These lengths form a Pythagorean triple. Therefore, the interior triangle is right. Its area is \[ \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 5 \cdot 12 = 30. \] Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Blake and Jenny each took four \(100\)-point tests. Blake averaged \(78\) on the four tests. Jenny scored \(10\) points higher than Blake on the first test, \(10\) points lower than him on the second test, and \(20\) points higher on both the third and fourth tests. What is the difference between Jenny’s average and Blake’s average on these four tests?
hints: Add Jenny’s four score differences from Blake’s.
Divide the total difference by \(4\) to compare averages.
problems.solution: The total point difference between the two is \[ 10 - 10 + 20 \cdot 2 = 40. \] The average of this difference is \(40 \div 4 = 10.\) Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: Problems \(8,\) \(9,\) and \(10\) use the data found in the accompanying paragraph and figures. Bake Sale Four friends, Art, Roger, Paul and Trisha, bake cookies, and all cookies have the same thickness. The shapes of the cookies differ, as shown. • Art’s cookies are trapezoids: • Roger’s cookies are rectangles: • Paul’s cookies are parallelograms: • Trisha’s cookies are triangles: Each friend uses the same amount of dough, and Art makes exactly \(12\) cookies. Who gets the fewest cookies from one batch of cookie dough?

options.label: E
options.content: There is a tie for fewest.

hints: Same dough and thickness means larger cookie area gives fewer cookies.
Compare the areas of the four cookie shapes.
problems.solution: Since the cookies all have the same thickness and use the same amount of dough, the largest cookie shape produces the fewest cookies. Art’s trapezoid has area \(\frac12(3+5)\cdot3=12.\) Roger’s rectangle has area \(4\cdot2=8.\) Paul’s parallelogram has area \(3\cdot2=6,\) and Trisha’s triangle has area \(\frac12\cdot3\cdot4=6.\) Art has the largest cookie area, so Art gets the fewest cookies from one batch. Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: Art’s cookies sell for \(60\)¢ each. To earn the same amount from a single batch, how much should one of Roger’s cookies cost?
hints: First find the total money Art earns from a batch.
Use the number of Roger’s cookies from the shared dough amount.
problems.solution: Art makes \(12\) cookies that sell for \(60\) cents each, so one batch earns \(12\cdot60=720\) cents. The batch has \(12\cdot12=144\) square inches of dough area, and each Roger cookie has area \(4\cdot2=8.\) Thus Roger makes \(144\div8=18\) cookies. To earn \(720\) cents from \(18\) cookies, each Roger cookie should cost \(720\div18=40\) cents. Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: How many cookies will be in one batch of Trisha’s cookies?
hints: Trisha’s cookie area is half of Art’s cookie area.
Same dough amount means half-size cookies make twice as many.
problems.solution: Art’s cookie area is \(12\) square inches, so the whole batch has area \(12\cdot12=144\) square inches. Trisha’s triangular cookie has area \(\frac12\cdot3\cdot4=6\) square inches. Therefore Trisha can make \(144\div6=24\) cookies per batch. Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Business is a little slow at Lou’s Fine Shoes, so Lou decides to have a sale. On Friday, Lou increases all of Thursday’s prices by \(10 \%.\) Over the weekend, Lou advertises the sale: “Ten percent off the listed price. Sale starts Monday.” How much does a pair of shoes cost on Monday that cost \(\$40\) on Thursday?
hints: The Monday discount is taken from Friday’s increased price.
Multiply the original price by \(1.10,\) then by \(0.90.\)
problems.solution: On Friday, the shoes are marked up by \(10\%,\) so the listed price becomes \(40\cdot1.10=44\) dollars. On Monday, the \(10\%\) discount is taken from \(\$44,\) giving \(44\cdot0.90=39.60\) dollars. Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: When a fair six-sided die is tossed on a table top, the bottom face cannot be seen. What is the probability that the product of the numbers on the five faces that can be seen is divisible by \(6?\)
hints: Check the only case where the face numbered \(6\) is hidden.
If \(6\) is hidden, the visible faces still include \(2\) and \(3.\)
problems.solution: If the face numbered \(6\) is visible, then the visible product is divisible by \(6.\) If the face numbered \(6\) is on the bottom, then the visible faces include both \(2\) and \(3,\) so their product is still divisible by \(6.\) Every possible toss works, so the probability is \(1.\) Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Fourteen white cubes are put together to form the figure on the right. The complete surface of the figure, including the bottom, is painted red. The figure is then separated into individual cubes. How many of the individual cubes have exactly four red faces?
hints: A cube has four painted faces exactly when it touches two other cubes.
Separate the top cubes, bottom corner cubes, and remaining cubes.
problems.solution: A cube has exactly four painted faces exactly when it is attached to exactly two other cubes. The \(4\) top cubes touch only one other cube, so they have \(5\) painted faces. The \(4\) bottom corner cubes touch three other cubes, so they have \(3\) painted faces. The remaining \(14-4-4=6\) cubes each touch exactly two other cubes, so they have exactly four painted faces. Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: In this addition problem, each letter stands for a different digit. \[\begin{array}{cccc}&T & W & O\\ +&T & W & O\\ \hline F& O & U & R\end{array}\] If \(T = 7\) and the letter \(O\) represents an even number, what is the only possible value for \(W?\)
hints: Use the hundreds column after \(T = 7.\)
The ones column and the fact that \(O\) is even force \(O.\)
problems.solution: Since both \(T\)’s are \(7,\) we get that \(O\) is either \(4\) or \(5.\) Since \(O\) is even, we get that \(O = 4.\) Then, we get that \(R = 4 + 4 = 8.\) We also know that \(W + W\) doesn’t carry over, since otherwise \(O\) would be \(5.\) Therefore, \(W\) is less than \(5\) and cannot be \(4\) or \(1.\) If \(W = 0,\) then \(U = 0,\) which gives two letters the same digit. If \(W = 2,\) then \(U = 4,\) which is also not allowed. This makes \(W = 3.\) Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: A figure is constructed from unit cubes. Each cube shares at least one face with another cube. What is the minimum number of cubes needed to build a figure with the front and side views shown?
hints: Try to satisfy both views with only three cubes.
A four-cube construction is shown; you only need to rule out three.
problems.solution: The front view requires an L-shape with three visible positions, so at least three cubes are needed. Suppose there were exactly three cubes. The two cubes that appear one above the other must share a face, so they have the same depth. The third cube appears beside the lower one. To share a face with either of the first two cubes, it must share the lower cube’s depth as well; otherwise it would be disconnected from both. Thus all three cubes would occupy one depth column, giving a one-column side view instead of the required L-shape. The shown four-cube construction has both required views, so the minimum is \(4.\) Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: Ali, Bonnie, Carlo and Dianna are going to drive together to a nearby theme park. The car they are using has four seats: one driver’s seat, one front passenger seat and two back seats. Bonnie and Carlo are the only two who can drive the car. How many possible seating arrangements are there?
hints: Choose the driver first.
After the driver is chosen, arrange the other three people in the remaining seats.
problems.solution: There are \(2\) options for who sits in the driver’s seat. There are \(3\) options for the other front seat, and \(2\) options for the first back seat. The last person has to sit in the last seat, for a total of \[ 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 12 \] possible seating arrangements. Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question:
The six children listed below are from two families of three siblings each. Each child has blue or brown eyes and black or blond hair. Children from the same family have at least one of these characteristics in common. Which two children are Jim’s siblings?
Child Eye Color Hair Color
Benjamin Blue Black
Jim Brown Blond
Nadeen Brown Black
Austin Blue Blond
Tevyn Blue Black
Sue Blue Blond
hints: Jim’s siblings must each share eye color or hair color with Jim.
The two siblings must also share at least one characteristic with each other.
problems.solution: Note that Nadeen, Austin, and Sue are the only individuals who share a characteristic with Jim. We need to find which of the \(3\) are completely different from the others. Austin and Sue both have blue eyes, which makes Nadeen the odd one out. Therefore, Austin and Sue are Jim’s siblings. Thus, E is the correct answer.

problems.question: Each of the twenty dots on the graph below represents one of Sarah’s classmates. Classmates who are friends are connected with a line segment. For her birthday party, Sarah is inviting only the following: all of her friends and all of those classmates who are friends with at least one of her friends. How many classmates will not be invited to Sarah’s party?
hints: Sarah invites vertices at distance \(1\) or \(2\) from her.
Count the dots not within two line segments of Sarah.
problems.solution: Sarah invites her friends and the classmates who are friends with at least one of her friends. In graph terms, she invites dots that are \(1\) or \(2\) line segments away from Sarah. From the graph, \(4\) dots are disconnected from Sarah’s component, and \(2\) more dots in Sarah’s component are \(3\) segments away. Those \(4+2=6\) classmates will not be invited. Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: How many integers between \(1000\) and \(2000\) have all three of the numbers \(15,\) \(20,\) and \(25\) as factors?
hints: Use the least common multiple of \(15,\) \(20,\) and \(25.\)
Count the multiples of that LCM between \(1000\) and \(2000.\)
problems.solution: If a number \(x\) has these three numbers as factors, then their least common multiple must also divide \(x.\) These numbers have the following prime factorizations: \[ 15 = 3 \cdot 5,\]\[ 20 = 2^2 \cdot 5,\]\[ 25 = 5^2. \] From these values, we get that the least common multiple is \[ 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2 = 300. \] Therefore, the multiples of \(300\) between \(1000\) and \(2000\) are \(1200,\) \(1500,\) and \(1800.\) Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: What is the measure of the acute angle formed by the hands of a clock at \(4{:}20\) a.m.?
hints: At \(4{:}20,\) the minute hand points at \(4.\)
The hour hand has moved one third of the way from \(4\) to \(5.\)
problems.solution: At \(4{:}20,\) the hour hand will be \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the way between \(4\) and \(5.\) Each hour represents \(360 \div 12 = 30^{\circ}.\) This means the hour hand will be \(30 \div 3 = 10^{\circ}\) past \(4.\) At \(20\) minutes, the minute hand points to \(4,\) so the acute angle between the hands is \(10^{\circ}.\) Thus, D is the correct answer.

problems.question: The area of trapezoid \(ABCD\) is \(164\text{ cm}^2.\) The altitude is \(8\) cm, \(AB\) is \(10\) cm, and \(CD\) is \(17\) cm. What is \(BC,\) in centimeters?
hints: Drop perpendiculars from \(B\) and \(C\) to the base.
Use the \(6-8-10\) and \(8-15-17\) right triangles.
problems.solution: Drop perpendiculars from \(B\) and \(C\) to \(\overline{AD},\) meeting it at \(E\) and \(F.\) In the left and right right triangles, \(AE=\sqrt{10^2-8^2}=6\) and \(FD=\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=15.\) The two side triangles have areas \(\frac12\cdot6\cdot8=24\) and \(\frac12\cdot15\cdot8=60.\) The middle rectangle has area \(8\cdot BC.\) Thus \(164=24+60+8BC,\) so \(8BC=80\) and \(BC=10.\) Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: The following figures are composed of squares and circles. Which figure has a shaded region with largest area?
hints: Figures \(A\) and \(B\) leave the same shaded area.
For \(C,\) compare \(\pi-2\) with \(4-\pi.\)
problems.solution: In figure \(A,\) the shaded area is the area of a \(2\) by \(2\) square minus a circle of radius \(1,\) so it is \(4-\pi.\) Figure \(B\) is made of four copies of figure \(A\) with half the side length, so each copy has one-fourth the area and the total shaded area is also \(4-\pi.\) In figure \(C,\) the circle has radius \(1,\) and the inscribed square has diagonal \(2,\) so its area is \(2.\) The shaded area is \(\pi-2.\) Since \(\pi>3,\) we have \(\pi-2>4-\pi,\) so figure \(C\) has the largest shaded area. Thus, C is the correct answer.

problems.question: In the pattern below, the cat moves clockwise through the four squares and the mouse moves counterclockwise through the eight exterior segments of the four squares. If the pattern is continued, where would the cat and mouse be after the \(247\)th move?
hints: The cat repeats every \(4\) moves.
The mouse repeats every \(8\) moves; use the remainders of \(247.\)
problems.solution: The cat’s position repeats every \(4\) moves, and the mouse’s position repeats every \(8\) moves. Since \(247\equiv3\pmod{4},\) the cat is in the same position as after the \(3\)rd move: the lower right square. Since \(247\equiv7\pmod{8},\) the mouse is in the same position as after the \(7\)th move: the left side of the lower left square. Thus, A is the correct answer.

problems.question: A ship travels from point \(A\) to point \(B\) along a semicircular path, centered at Island \(X.\) Then it travels along a straight path from \(B\) to \(C.\) Which of these graphs best shows the ship’s distance from Island \(X\) as it moves along its course?
hints: Along the semicircle, the distance from \(X\) is constant.
On the straight segment, the ship first gets closer to \(X,\) then farther away.
problems.solution: Every point on the semicircular path from \(A\) to \(B\) is the same distance from the center \(X,\) so the graph starts horizontally. On the straight path from \(B\) to \(C,\) the ship first gets closer to \(X\) and then farther away from \(X.\) Only graph \(B\) starts flat and then decreases before increasing. Thus, B is the correct answer.

problems.question: In the figure, the area of square \(WXYZ\) is \(25 \text{ cm}^2.\) The four smaller squares have sides \(1\) cm long, either parallel to or coinciding with the sides of the large square. In \(\triangle ABC,\) \(AB = AC,\) and when \(\triangle ABC\) is folded over side \(\overline{BC},\) point \(A\) coincides with \(O,\) the center of square \(WXYZ.\) What is the area of \(\triangle ABC,\) in square centimeters?
hints: Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(\overline{BC}.\)
Folding makes the distance from \(A\) to \(\overline{BC}\) equal the distance from \(O\) to \(\overline{BC}.\)
problems.solution: The side length of \(WXYZ\) is \(5\) cm, since \(\sqrt{25} = 5.\) We also know that the distance from \(\overline{WZ}\) to \(\overline{BC}\) is \(2\) since it is the sum of the side lengths of \(2\) unit squares. Finally, the distance from \(A\) to \(\overline{BC}\) is the same as the distance from \(\overline{BC}\) to \(O,\) which is \[ 2 + \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{9}{2} \text{ cm}. \] Now, we can find \(BC,\) which is \[ WZ - 2 = 5 - 2 = 3 \text{ cm}. \] Therefore, the area of \(\triangle ABC\) is \[ \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 3 \cdot \dfrac{9}{2} = \dfrac{27}{4} \text{ cm}^2. \] Thus, C is the correct answer.
